::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("ps > .21", "p = .24", "p = .996"), Sentence = c("Specifically, there was no effect of Session in the youngest children (all 4-year-old ps > .21), but it emerged and became stronger with age (5and 6-year-old ps < .047).", "The strength of shared co-occurrence connections was predicted by all factors (ps < .05) except direct co-occurrence connections between the pseudoadjective and familiar noun (p = .24).", "Follow-up holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons indicated that the effect of age was driven by a significant improvement in shared co-occurrence connections from age 5 to 6 (p < .001), whereas ages 4 and 5 did not significantly differ (p = .996; see Supplemental Materials for further exploratory analyses of change with age)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Much of human knowledge distills patterns that are consistent across many similar experiences over time, such as the typical layout of a bedroom.
This is particularly true of word knowledge.

The thousands of words we learn form a stable, interconnected network of word meanings that capture regularities in the way words are typically combined to express ideas, such as that "oranges" are something you can "eat" and similar to "apples".
Yet, we know surprisingly little about accumulating knowledge from regularities over time, especially in childhood when building knowledge is paramount.
Here, we investigated 4-6-year-old children's abilities to accumulate interconnected word knowledge from regularities experienced repeatedly over a month.
Younger children appeared to relearn the regularities anew at each exposure, whereas older children accumulated increasingly strong connections across encounters.
These findings point to substantial developmental changes in gradual learning processes that build knowledge over time.

Childhood is a time of building a large, stable foundation of semantic knowledge about the world, from everyday routines (e.g., getting ready to go to school) to conceptual understanding (e.g., birds have wings) and facts about the environment (e.g., food is kept in kitchens).

Words make up a critical part of this knowledge by anchoring knowledge in the mind (Garrard, Ralph, Patterson, Pratt, & Hodges, 2005; Lupyan & Thompson-Schill, 2012) and providing the medium for communicating it with each other.
text.formatted: Words make up a critical part of this knowledge by anchoring knowledge in the mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Garrard, Ralph, Patterson, Pratt, & Hodges, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Lupyan & Thompson-Schill, 2012)</ref> and providing the medium for communicating it with each other.

text.text: Building word knowledge requires learning not just individual words, but also connections between them, such as that "oranges" are "yummy", something you can "eat", and similar to "apples".
These semantic connections pervade all aspects of language fluency.

For example, connections fill in the blanks common in everyday language, such as comprehending that "I'd love some of those oranges, they're so yummy" expresses a desire to "eat" oranges even though eating was never mentioned (Ouellette, 2006; Perfetti, 2007; Tannenbaum, Torgesen, & Wagner, 2006).
text.formatted: For example, connections fill in the blanks common in everyday language, such as comprehending that "I'd love some of those oranges, they're so yummy" expresses a desire to "eat" oranges even though eating was never mentioned <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Ouellette, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Perfetti, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Tannenbaum, Torgesen, & Wagner, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Semantic connections likewise fuel the limitless generativity of language by allowing us to generalize across words similar in meaning (e.g., Colunga & Smith, 2005), such as our ability to discuss "ripe apples" even if we have previously only heard about "ripe oranges".
text.formatted: Semantic connections likewise fuel the limitless generativity of language by allowing us to generalize across words similar in meaning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Colunga & Smith, 2005)</ref>, such as our ability to discuss "ripe apples" even if we have previously only heard about "ripe oranges".

text.text: Yet, despite the importance of these connections, we understand little about the development of semantic learning processes that build interconnected knowledge.
Intuitively, building stable semantic knowledge involves picking up on consistent regularities (e.g., noticing that getting dressed always happens before going to school).

When it comes to word knowledge, there is an emerging consensus that regularities of word co-occurrence constitute a potentially powerful source for semantic learning (Fourtassi, 2020; Huebner & Willits, 2018; Landauer & Dumais, 1997; Unger, Yim, Savic, Dennis, & Sloutsky, 2023).
text.formatted: When it comes to word knowledge, there is an emerging consensus that regularities of word co-occurrence constitute a potentially powerful source for semantic learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fourtassi, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Huebner & Willits, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Landauer & Dumais, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Unger, Yim, Savic, Dennis, & Sloutsky, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the remarkable successes of Large Language Models amply demonstrate the wealth of interconnected word knowledge that can be derived just from regularities in the way words occur with other words (Mikolov, Chen, Corrado, & Dean, 2013; Petroni et al., 2019; Webb, Holyoak, & Lu, 2023).
text.formatted: Indeed, the remarkable successes of Large Language Models amply demonstrate the wealth of interconnected word knowledge that can be derived just from regularities in the way words occur with other words <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Mikolov, Chen, Corrado, & Dean, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Petroni et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Webb, Holyoak, & Lu, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a learner could connect "orange" and "apple" to "yummy" based on the tendency of these words to directly cooccur with each other.
Moreover, a learner could integrate information across these direct co-occurrence regularities to connect "orange" to "apple" based on their shared pattern of cooccurrence with "yummy".

This distributional hypothesis (illustrated in Figure 1) highlights how direct co-occurrence regularities may foster connections between words that can be combined in meaningful expressions, and shared co-occurrence may foster connections between words similar in meaning.

text.text: Indeed, evidence suggests that child language input is rich in regularities in which words that can be meaningfully combined tend to directly co-occur, and words similar in meaning tend to share co-occurrence and often also directly co-occur (such as "dog" and "cat"; Fourtassi, 2020; Huebner & Willits, 2018; Li, Farkas, & MacWhinney, 2004; Peters & Borovsky, 2019; Unger et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Indeed, evidence suggests that child language input is rich in regularities in which words that can be meaningfully combined tend to directly co-occur, and words similar in meaning tend to share co-occurrence and often also directly co-occur (such as "dog" and "cat"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Fourtassi, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Huebner & Willits, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Li, Farkas, & MacWhinney, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Peters & Borovsky, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Unger et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, for children to acquire interconnected word knowledge from these regularities, they must be able to learn connections from language experienced on different occasions over time.
In just a single experience (such as a conversation or story), words might only co-occur once or a few times.
Moreover, even repeated co-occurrences might be idiosyncratic.
For example, a child might hear a story about a mouse who tries to eat a big apple in which "mouse" and "apple" repeatedly co-occur, but then never hear "mouse" and "apple" together again.

To instead pick up on co-occurrences that are consistent over time and contexts, a child must possess semantic learning mechanisms that at minimum: (A) retain some trace of past experiences, and (B) build upon these past traces from subsequent experiences (McClelland & Rogers, 2003).
text.formatted: To instead pick up on co-occurrences that are consistent over time and contexts, a child must possess semantic learning mechanisms that at minimum: (A) retain some trace of past experiences, and (B) build upon these past traces from subsequent experiences <ref type="bibr">(McClelland & Rogers, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: It is hardly controversial that some degree of semantic learning must begin early in childhood, as even young children have begun to learn words (Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2015) and connections between them (Arias-Trejo & Plunkett, 2009 , 2013; Styles & Plunkett, 2009; Willits, Wojcik, Seidenberg, & Saffran, 2013) that play a vital role in organizing word knowledge (e.g., Borovsky, Ellis, Evans, & Elman, 2016).

text.text: Indeed, some have proposed that a semantic learning system that builds knowledge from repeated experiences over time is the foundational memory system of the mind and emerges early in child development (Gómez & Figure 1.

text.text: Co-occurrence regularities that can foster semantic connections between words.
Edgin, 2016; Newcombe, Benear, Ngo, & Olson, 2024; Ngo, Benear, Popal, Olson, & Newcombe, 2021).

text.text: Yet, we have surprisingly little insight into the emergence of learning that accumulates knowledge across experiences.

Prior investigations into children's sensitivity to cooccurrence regularities have instead focused on learning from a single one-off experience (e.g. Hay, Pelucchi, Estes, & Saffran, 2011; Saffran, Aslin, & Newport, 1996; Savic, Unger, & Sloutsky, 2022; Wojcik & Saffran, 2015).
text.formatted: Prior investigations into children's sensitivity to cooccurrence regularities have instead focused on learning from a single one-off experience (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hay, Pelucchi, Estes, & Saffran, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Saffran, Aslin, & Newport, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Savic, Unger, & Sloutsky, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wojcik & Saffran, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the few studies of learning over time in development have primarily compared adults to older (8-12-year-old) children on a disparate variety of learning phenomena (Bishop, Barry, & Hardiman, 2012; James, Gaskell, & Henderson, 2019; Smalle, Page, Duyck, Edwards, & Szmalec, 2018).
text.formatted: Moreover, the few studies of learning over time in development have primarily compared adults to older (8-12-year-old) children on a disparate variety of learning phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bishop, Barry, & Hardiman, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">James, Gaskell, & Henderson, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Smalle, Page, Duyck, Edwards, & Szmalec, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although these studies intriguingly suggest that late childhood may be a period when the benefits of repeated experience are particularly strong, late childhood is preceded by years of development.
We therefore do not know whether knowledge accumulation develops early, or results from substantial developmental change.
In what follows, we review evidence from single-session studies, highlight the critical importance of accumulating knowledge over time, and present a systematic investigation into its development.

To assess connections formed from direct and shared co-occurrence, a typical approach is to present participants with triads of items in which one item (item A) separately co-occurs with two other items (B and C).

Subsequently, participants are tested on their formation of connections between items that directly cooccur (A-B, A-C) and share patterns of cooccurrence (B-C) (Bauer & San Souci, 2010; Benton, 2026; Benton, Rakison, & Sobel, 2021; Miller-Goldwater, Cronin-Golomb, Porter, & Bauer, 2021; Savic et al., 2022; Schlichting, Guarino, Roome, & Preston, 2021; Schlichting, Guarino, Schapiro, Turk-Browne, & Preston, 2017; Yermolayeva & Rakison, 2016).
text.formatted: Subsequently, participants are tested on their formation of connections between items that directly cooccur (A-B, A-C) and share patterns of cooccurrence (B-C) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bauer & San Souci, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Benton, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Benton, Rakison, & Sobel, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Miller-Goldwater, Cronin-Golomb, Porter, & Bauer, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Savic et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Schlichting, Guarino, Roome, & Preston, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Schlichting, Guarino, Schapiro, Turk-Browne, & Preston, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Yermolayeva & Rakison, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Across studies that have used this approach, a consistent developmental picture has emerged.
An ability to pick up on direct co-occurrence emerges early in childhood (see also Wojcik & Saffran, 2015) and continues to improve with age.
text.formatted: An ability to pick up on direct co-occurrence emerges early in childhood (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wojcik & Saffran, 2015)</ref> and continues to improve with age.

text.text: If children learned like the language models highlighted above, then forming connections between items that co-occur would automatically foster connections between items that shared co-occurrence.
Yet, this does not appear to be the case.

Learning that both B and C directly co-occur with A is insufficient to also connect B and C. Instead, abilities to form connections from direct co-occurrence appear to be gradually supplemented by abilities to integrate across these connections to form shared co-occurrence connections.

For example, in Savic et al.'s 2022 studies of forming connections between A-B-C triads of words embedded in sentences, even 4-year-olds formed connections based on direct co-occurrence, but only older children and adults also reliably integrated across direct co-occurrences to form connections based on shared co-occurrence.
These findings reveal that it is not enough for regularities to be part of everyday experience: instead, abilities to form connections from these regularities must also develop.
While these studies shed light on forming connections from a single experience, building interconnected word knowledge is a necessarily protracted process.
As explained above, any one experience may contain few co-occurrences, and even repeated co-occurrences within an experience may be idiosyncratic.
Therefore, semantic learning processes that build knowledge from regularities should accumulate such knowledge as regularities are experienced repeatedly across experiences.

Indeed, it is possible that failure to engage such learning processes accounts for the relatively poor learning in young children observed in prior single-session studies (particularly for connections based on shared co-occurrence), such that even young children might learn well given multiple experiences with the same regularities.
Yet we know little about the development of semantic learning processes that accumulate word knowledge over time.

Because some semantic knowledge begins to emerge even in infancy, it has been posited that semantic learning is robust from early in development (Gómez & Edgin, 2016; Newcombe et al., 2024; Ngo et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Because some semantic knowledge begins to emerge even in infancy, it has been posited that semantic learning is robust from early in development <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gómez & Edgin, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Newcombe et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ngo et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, few studies have actually examined semantic learning in childhood.

In apparent support of early semantic learning, a handful of studies point to better knowledge accumulation in late childhood (8-12 years) than in adults (e.g., James et al., 2019; Smalle et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In apparent support of early semantic learning, a handful of studies point to better knowledge accumulation in late childhood (8-12 years) than in adults (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">James et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Smalle et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, these studies focused on older children with years of development behind them.
Moreover, these studies only examined children's knowledge for the material that they directly experienced, and not abilities to build knowledge across experiences.

In contrast, one recent study comparing knowledge accumulation in younger children to adults points to substantial developmental change. Savic et al. (2022) compared the strength of connections formed in 4-year-olds after hearing the stories embedded with A-B-C triads across multiple days to those formed in adults after a single day.

(2022)</ref> compared the strength of connections formed in 4-year-olds after hearing the stories embedded with A-B-C triads across multiple days to those formed in adults after a single day.

text.text: Although multiple repetitions led 4-year-olds to form direct co-occurrence connections similar to strength to those formed from one session in adults, unlike adults, they failed to form shared co-occurrence connections.
This finding points to a failure in young children to capitalize on opportunities to build semantic knowledge over time.

However, because the focus of the Savic et al. (2022) study was on contrasting the formation of direct and shared co-occurrence connec-tions in children and adults, it was not designed to illuminate the development of knowledge accumulation.
text.formatted: However, because the focus of the <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Savic et al. (2022)</ref> study was on contrasting the formation of direct and shared co-occurrence connec-tions in children and adults, it was not designed to illuminate the development of knowledge accumulation.

text.text: Specifically, this study contrasted two different amounts of exposure at two distant points in development: a single session of exposure in adults versus repeated exposure over days in 4-year-olds.

Furthermore, the task for each session probed only the connections that spontaneously came to mind, rather than the full set of direct and shared A-B, A-C and B-C connections that could be formed, and a targeted evaluation of shared co-occurrence connections only took place after the final session.
Moreover, there was no assessment of whether young children and adults similarly understood the task.
Therefore, this study does not provide a systematic investigation of the development of accumulating knowledge of connections across experiences.
Together, contrasting these few studies with younger and older children hints that semantic learning may undergo substantial developmental change, but does not reveal the nature of this change.
The present study aimed to illuminate the development of a fundamental property of semantic learning: the accumulation of knowledge from regularities experienced over time.

We tackled this aim using a version of the A-B-C approach described above in which children were repeatedly exposed to direct and shared co-occurrence regularities over time, embedded in stories that children heard in three sessions across one month.

In contrast with the handful of prior studies on learning over time, we examined the accumulation of knowledge from one session to the next (c.f. Savic et al., 2022) and how this accumulation may change across childhood (c.f. Bishop et al., 2012; James et al., 2019; Savic et al., 2022; Smalle et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In contrast with the handful of prior studies on learning over time, we examined the accumulation of knowledge from one session to the next (c.f. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Savic et al., 2022)</ref> and how this accumulation may change across childhood (c.f. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bishop et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">James et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Savic et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Smalle et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We focused on developmental changes between the ages of four and six because it is a period of substantial changes in children's interconnected word knowledge (Crowe & Prescott, 2003; Storm, 1980; Unger, Fisher, Nugent, Ventura, & MacLellan, 2016) and abilities to form connections from a single bout of exposure to regularities (Miller-Goldwater et al., 2021; Savic et al., 2022; Schlichting et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We focused on developmental changes between the ages of four and six because it is a period of substantial changes in children's interconnected word knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Crowe & Prescott, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Storm, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Unger, Fisher, Nugent, Ventura, & MacLellan, 2016)</ref> and abilities to form connections from a single bout of exposure to regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Miller-Goldwater et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Savic et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Schlichting et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: From previous studies of learning from a single bout of exposure, we expected that the very first session would reveal an early-emerging ability to form connections from direct cooccurrences that improves with age and is gradually supplemented by an ability to integrate connections from shared co-occurrence.
Critically, our design allowed us to investigate developmental changes in building and strengthening these connections with repeated exposure over time.
Such developmental changes would point to the maturation of semantic learning systems responsible for extracting knowledge from everyday regularities.
Participants were 4, 5, and 6-year-olds recruited in the US via social media posts.

Following exclusions based on performance on "control" trials assessing attentiveness and task com-prehension (see below), final sample sizes were: 27 4-year-olds (range = 4.01 -4.92, M = 4.48, SD = 0.26), 29 5-year-olds (range = 5.00 -5.97, M = 5.549, SD = 0.28), and 32 6-year-olds (range = 6.03 -6.96, M = 6.46, SD = 0.31).

The proportion of children who failed to meet the criteria for attentiveness and task comprehension was higher for younger children, such that the numbers of participants excluded were 16 four-year-olds, 8 five-year-olds and 2 six-yearolds.
The demographic makeup was 74% White, 16% Multiracial, 6% Black, 2% Asian and 2% unspecified, of whom 57% were female, 41% male and 2% other or unspecified.
Triads.

The primary materials were two triads of words (Figure 2 A.) Each triad contained a novel pseudoadjective (e.g., "foobly") paired with a familiar noun (e.g., "apple") and a novel pseudonoun (e.g., "mipp").

text.text: Thus, each triad contained two pairs of words embedded in a short story as described below, for a total of four word pairs.
Story.
Word pairs from triads were embedded within sentences that were combined to form a short story (Figure 2 B).
text.formatted: Word pairs from triads were embedded within sentences that were combined to form a short story (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2 B</ref>).

text.text: Sentences were uninformative about the meanings of novel pseudowords, such as "Yesterday I saw a foobly apple".
Thus, the only information about the con-nections between triad pseudowords and their meanings came from the regularities with which triad words were used in sentences.
The four pairs were each embedded within 10 different sentences (40 sentences in total).

Pilot work suggested that children in the youngest age group (age 4) might struggle to learn even the simpler connections based on direct co-occurrence when all four word pairs were mingled throughout the story.
The simplified variant of the task that most consistently led to above-floor performance in 4-year-old pilot participants presented the story in two non-counterbalanced parts.

Part 1 presented 20 sentences containing the pairs in which the pseudoadjective directly co-occurred with the familiar noun, and Part 2 presented 20 sentences containing pairs in which the pseudoadjective directly co-occurred with the pseudonoun.
All sentences were recorded by a female native English speaker.
We developed an additional set of sentences for use in a "Muffled Test" designed to test whether children formed connections based on direct co-occurrence (see Procedure and Figure 3).

text.text: Muffled Test sentences were similar to the story sentences, but in each sentence, one of the words in a pair was masked by a static sound, as in "I'd love to see a [STATIC] mipp".
As described in the Procedure, children were asked to choose the masked word from two options.
We developed four sentences to test the formation of connections between each pair (16 sentences in total), in which half masked the pseudoadjective and half masked the familiar or pseudonoun.

The "Label Test" was designed to test whether participants connected the familiar noun to both (a) the pseu-doadjective in the same triad based on direct co-occurrence, and (b) the pseudonoun in the same triad based on shared co-occurrence.
We used four pictures of each familiar noun from the triads (i.e., apple and horse).

As described below and in Figure 3, each picture was presented with one prompt to assess connections based on direct co-occurrence, and another prompt to assess connections based on shared co-occurrence.

text.text: Control Items.
Importantly, we developed a set of "control" items for both the Muffled and Labeled tests to check that participants were attentive and understood the tasks.
Recall that each test assessed whether children formed connections between a pseudoadjective and a noun in the same triad, or a pseudonoun and a noun in the same triad.

To match this structure, control items consisted of a familiar adjective and two familiar nouns that are already likely to be connected in young children's vocabularies, such as "furry"-"dog" and "cat"-"dog".
Items were high-frequency words that reliably co-occur in children's everyday language input (see Supplemental Materials).
As shown in Figure 4, control items for Muffled Test were presented during the Muffled Test Warmup, whereas control items for the Label Test were interleaved with test items during testing.

text.text: Participants completed three sessions on separate days within one month (with an average gap of 6 days between sessions).
Sessions followed the sequence shown in Figure 4, in which children were exposed to regularities in language and their formation of connections was assessed.

text.text: Sessions were hosted on the online Gorilla platform, took place on Zoom and were guided by an experimenter.
Introduction and Muffled Test Warmup.
Participants were introduced to Izzy, a cartoon alien who tells travel stories.
Participants then completed a warmup version of the Muffled Test that was subsequently used to assess children's formation of connections based on direct co-occurrence (see below).
The warmup consisted entirely of control trials made up of familiar words.
Children were first told that Izzy was going to say some things over the radio in her spaceship, but that the radio sometimes makes a funny sound.
The experimenter would give the child two word choices, and the child would pick the one that Izzy probably said when the radio made the funny sound.

The experimenter then played an example sentence, in which Izzy said "My mom saw a [STATIC] butterfly", and the experimenter explained that if the word choices were "pretty" and "sharp", the best answer would be "pretty", because "pretty butterfly" makes sense.

Children then completed four trials of this warmup version of the Muffled Task using Control Item familiar words, such as hearing "I'd really love a [STATIC] cookie" and being asked whether the muffled word was "yummy" or "wet".
Story and Muffled Test.
Participants were told that Izzy would tell them a travel story using some fun alien words.
Participants then completed this phase in two parts.

The Part 1 Story and Muffled Test presented and assessed connections between the pseudoadjective and familiar noun from the two triads, and Part 2 presented and assessed connections between the pseudoadjective and pseudonoun from the two triads.
Parts 1 and 2 had the same format.
The experimenter first played audio clips of the pseudowords used in that part, and prompted the child to repeat them.
Next, participants heard the story and completed the Muffled Test.
Each part of Muffled Test contained 8 trials in the same format as the warmup (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: Each part of Muffled Test contained 8 trials in the same format as the warmup (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).

text.text: In each trial, children heard one sentence in which an audible word from a triad was accompanied by an audio clip of static.
Children were prompted to choose between a word from the same triad as the audible word, and a word from a different triad.
For example, when the familiar noun was audible, the choices were the pseudoadjective from the same versus different triad.
Accordingly, the Muffled Test assessed connections based on direct co-occurrence of words from the same triad.
Label Test.
For the label test, the experimenter explained that Izzy had taken pictures on her travels, and asked the child to help Izzy describe them.
On each trial, participants saw a picture and were asked to label it with one of two word options: either one of the two pseudoadjectives, or one of the two pseudonouns.

Trials in which the two options were pseudoadjectives measured the formation of connections based on direct co-occurrence from the accuracy with which participants label pictures of a familiar noun (e.g., apple) using the pseudoadjective with which it directly co-occurred (e.g., "foobly").
The same logic applies for measuring the formation of connections based on shared cooccurrence from accuracy on pseudonoun trials (e.g., using "mipp" to label apples).

To ensure that children were asked to use the pseudowords as labels in a way that is grammatical in English, for pseudoadjectives, children were asked, "Is this one [pseudoadjective 1] or [pseudoadjective 2]?", and for pseudonouns, children were asked, "Is this one like a [pseudonoun 1] or a [pseudonoun 2]?".
Control trials used the same format and prompted children to label pictures with familiar adjectives and nouns, such as labeling a dog as "furry" versus "yummy", and like a "cat" versus "ice cream".
Participants completed 8 trials measuring connections based on direct and shared co-occurrence, and 6 control trials.
Primary analyses measured the contributions of age and/or repeated exposure across sessions to forming connections based on direct and shared co-occurrence.
Analyses were performed as generalized linear mixed effects models on raw accuracy data using the lme4 package in R (Bates, Maechler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015).

Following exclusions, although performance on control trials overlapped substantially across age groups, performance in the youngest age group remained somewhat lower than performance in the oldest age group (see Supplemental Materials for further details).

To partially mitigate this concern, all analyses below included performance on control trials as a covariate, to estimate age group differences on test trials given comparable control trial performance.
A primary goal of the present study was to investigate the development of accumulating knowledge from exposure to co-occurrence regularities over time.

We therefore examined the effects of Age (4-, 5-, or 6-year-old) and Session (1, 2, or 3) and their interaction for each of the measures of connections that could be formed based on co-occurrence (with control trial performance included as a covariate).

As described in the Introduction, forming connections based on direct co-occurrence is a prerequisite for forming connections based on shared co-occurrence.

However, findings from single-session studies suggest that forming connections based on shared co-occurrence further depends on developing abilities to integrate across direct co-occurrence connections.
The present study allowed us to gain further insight into the prerequisites for forming connections based on shared co-occurrence.
Here, shared co-occurrence connections could be formed based on the direct co-occurrence of a pseudoadjective with both a familiar noun and a pseudonoun (Figure 3).

text.text: We thus tested whether the strength of shared co-occurrence connections was predicted by: (1) the strength of direct co-occurrence connections measured in the same session, (2) repeated exposure to regularities across sessions, and (3) age.
This model was specified as: shared ∼ direct pseudo-familiar + direct pseudo-pseudo + session + age

Human word knowledge is fundamentally interconnected.

The remarkable successes of language models have shown that in principle, much of the richly interconnected word knowledge that humans develop can be derived from co-occurrence regularities abundant in everyday language (Landauer & Dumais, 1997; Petroni et al., 2019; Webb et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The remarkable successes of language models have shown that in principle, much of the richly interconnected word knowledge that humans develop can be derived from co-occurrence regularities abundant in everyday language <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Landauer & Dumais, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Petroni et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Webb et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, like language models, children might also build richly interconnected word knowledge from regularities in everyday language.

To capitalize on these regularities, children must retain what they have learned from the language they experience on one day and build upon it from the language they experience on another (McClelland & Rogers, 2003).
text.formatted: To capitalize on these regularities, children must retain what they have learned from the language they experience on one day and build upon it from the language they experience on another <ref type="bibr">(McClelland & Rogers, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: For the first time, we show that abilities to build up interconnected word knowledge with experience change substantially over childhood.
Children in the youngest age group did form some connections starting from their first exposure, but showed no evidence of building upon these connections with repeated exposures.
With age, children formed increasingly strong connections from one exposure to the next.

Although younger children might accumulate stronger connections with the many hours of language they experience daily over weeks, months and years, the current findings indicate that this accumulation becomes faster and more robust with age.

Therefore, the increasingly interconnected word knowledge that emerges in development may come in part from the interplay between repeated exposures to regularities of word use and developmental improvements in abilities to capitalize on these exposures.
The present findings shed new light on the development of learning processes that build knowledge over time.

The interconnected word knowledge studied here is part of the stable base of semantic knowledge about the world that is amassed over the course of childhood and into adulthood (McClelland & Rogers, 2003; Tulving, 1972).
text.formatted: The interconnected word knowledge studied here is part of the stable base of semantic knowledge about the world that is amassed over the course of childhood and into adulthood <ref type="bibr">(McClelland & Rogers, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Tulving, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Acquiring this knowledge is commonly attributed to a learning system that is inherently gradual.

For example, the popular Complementary Learning Systems theory (Ku-maran, Hassabis, & McClelland, 2016; McClelland, McNaughton, & O'Reilly, 1995) proposes that experiences are processed in two learning systems: a fast, episodic system that rapidly stores individual experiences, and a slow semantic system that gradually picks up on regularities that are consistent across experiences.
text.formatted: For example, the popular Complementary Learning Systems theory <ref type="bibr">(Ku-maran, Hassabis, & McClelland, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McClelland, McNaughton, & O'Reilly, 1995)</ref> proposes that experiences are processed in two learning systems: a fast, episodic system that rapidly stores individual experiences, and a slow semantic system that gradually picks up on regularities that are consistent across experiences.

text.text: The semantic system is characterized as having particular features that allow it to accumulate a stable knowledge base rather than memories for idiosyncratic experiences, including a slow learning rate and a dependence on consolidation in memory between one experience and the next.
When it comes to development, there are multiple proposals that the semantic system emerges and matures relatively early in childhood (Gómez & Edgin, 2016; Ngo et al., 2021).
text.formatted: When it comes to development, there are multiple proposals that the semantic system emerges and matures relatively early in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gómez & Edgin, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ngo et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This idea is grounded in evidence that even infants and toddlers are sensitive to some kinds of statistical regularities (e.g., Saffran et al., 1996; Wojcik & Saffran, 2015) and begin to accumulate some semantic knowledge (e.g., learn some words and semantic connections between them, Arias-Trejo & Plunkett, 2009; Bergelson & Aslin, 2017; Bergelson & Swingley, 2012).
text.formatted: This idea is grounded in evidence that even infants and toddlers are sensitive to some kinds of statistical regularities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Saffran et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wojcik & Saffran, 2015)</ref> and begin to accumulate some semantic knowledge (e.g., learn some words and semantic connections between them, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Arias-Trejo & Plunkett, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bergelson & Aslin, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bergelson & Swingley, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, although semantic learning processes might begin to emerge early on, prior evidence does not illuminate its development.

Prior evidence is particularly uninformative about the development of semantic learning that unfolds over real-world timescales, such as learning regularities that are repeatedly experienced from one day to another.
Thus, the present study provides new evidence that slow semantic learning systems continue to develop substantially across childhood, even after the age of four.

As in single-session studies of both language and other domains (Bauer & San Souci, 2010; Benton, 2026; Benton et al., 2021; Miller-Goldwater et al., 2021; Savic et al., 2022; Schlichting et al., 2021 Schlichting et al., , 2017;; Yermolayeva & Rakison, 2016), the present findings revealed an early-emerging sensitivity to direct co-occurrence (learning A-B and A-C) that improves and is supplemented by sensitivity to shared co-occurrence with age (learning A-C).

text.text: Although the exact ages when these sensitivities emerge and become robust may vary across domains (either due to real domain differences or more superficial differences between paradigms, such as number of connections to be learned), evidence consistently points to a later-emerging ability to form shared co-occurrence connections for which direct co-occurrence connections are necessary but insufficient.
However, the mechanisms underlying this later-emerging ability remain unclear.

Literature across domains has posited mechanisms of two broad types: (1) forming similar mental representations of items that share co-occurrence, and (2) chaining together direct co-occurrence connections that share an overlapping item (e.g., Banino, Koster, Hassabis, & Kumaran, 2016; Benton, 2026; Hall, Mitchell, Graham, & Lavis, 2003; Kumaran et al., 2016; McClelland et al., 1995; Schapiro, Turk-Browne, Botvinick, & Norman, 2017; Zeithamova & Bowman, 2020).

text.text: Alternatively, in the present study, integration could also involve a more language-specific ability to first infer meanings for the pseudoadjective (e.g., that "foobly" is a characteristic of fruits similar to "sweet" and "juicy" based on its direct cooccurrence with "apple") and then infer meanings for the pseudonouns (e.g., that "mipp" is a fruit based on its direct co-occurrence with "foobly" that has taken on a fruit-characteristic meaning) (e.g., Lany & Saffran, 2010).

text.text: Illuminating the mechanisms underpinning shared co-occurrence connections and whether they are the same or different across domains therefore represents a key target for future research.
The developmental changes in learning over time observed in the present study may help explain the way interconnected word knowledge evolves over childhood.

Early on, semantic connections often link words that directly co-occur, including "thematically" related words different in meaning that are associated with each other such as "dog" and "bone", and many "taxonomically" related words similar in meaning such as "dog" and "cat" (Blaye & Bonthoux, 2001; Fenson, Vella, & Kennedy, 1989; Fisher, 2010; Lin & Murphy, 2001; Lucariello, Kyratzis, & Nelson, 1992; Lucariello & Nelson, 1985; Matlen, Fisher, & Godwin, 2015; Sloutsky, Yim, Yao, & Dennis, 2017; Unger, Savic, & Sloutsky, 2020; Unger, Vales, & Fisher, 2020; Unger et al., 2023).

text.text: With age, these connections are supplemented by taxonomic connections between words that may not directly co-occur with each other, but are likely to share co-occurrence with other words (Lucariello et al., 1992; Unger, Savic, & Sloutsky, 2020; Wojcik & Kandhadai, 2019).
text.formatted: With age, these connections are supplemented by taxonomic connections between words that may not directly co-occur with each other, but are likely to share co-occurrence with other words <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lucariello et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Unger, Savic, & Sloutsky, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Wojcik & Kandhadai, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: There is a clear alignment between this pattern in semantic connections and the direct-before-shared pattern in semantic learning processes observed in the present study.
Thus, the developmental changes in learning processes observed here may in part drive the typical development of interconnected word knowledge.
Everyday experience is rich in regularities that can support learning meaningful connections between words.
To benefit from these regularities, a child must retain some trace of past experiences and build upon these traces with subsequent experiences.
The present findings reveal that such semantic learning develops substantially across childhood.
Thus, richly interconnected word knowledge may emerge from the interplay between repeated opportunities for learning and developing abilities to capitalize on these opportunities.
